books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, A. Reform Movements in the Antebellum Period

stimulus.text: "Education, then, beyond all other devices of human origin, is the great equalizer of the conditions of men, — the balance-wheel of the social machinery. . . . It does better than to disarm the poor of their hostility towards the rich: it prevents being poor." — Horace Mann, Twelfth Annual Report to the Massachusetts Board of Education, 1848
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Horace Mann, Twelfth Annual Report of the Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education (1848). Wording checked against the report text as reprinted in Life and Works of Horace Mann, vol. III (1868), p. 669, and the ETSU faculty transcription; ellipses mark omissions.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Mann, Twelfth Annual Report (1848)
stem: Mann calls education the "balance-wheel of the social machinery" mainly to argue that public schools can

options.text: teach factory skills and nothing else
options.misconception: Mann wants citizens, not just workers; his schools teach reading, morals, and civic duty.

options.text: level class differences and keep a republic healthy

options.misconception: Mann campaigned for free public schools; he never called for abolishing private ones.

options.text: educate only the children of the wealthy
options.misconception: Mann's schools are for all children; educating only the wealthy is the European system he rejects.

rationales.A: Mann's schools teach reading, writing, and citizenship, not factory skills alone. His goal is republican citizens, not just trained hands.
rationales.B: A balance-wheel steadies a machine. Mann says universal education steadies society by giving poor children the means to resist the rich.
rationales.C: Mann built the public system up; he never proposed closing private schools. The choice was public schools for all, not schools for none.
rationales.D: Educating only the wealthy is the European theory Mann attacks. His Massachusetts theory gives every child an equal chance.
rationales.general:
1. Picture the machine. A balance-wheel keeps a machine running true instead of shaking apart.
2. Apply it to society. Without schools, wealth and poverty pull the republic apart.
3. Name Mann's claim. Universal education steadies the republic by lifting the poor.
Background: Mann served as secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education in the 1840s and campaigned for free common schools.
Remember: a metaphor is an argument — ask what the machine is and what steadies it.
